title: Chinese Chess WebMCP: How to Win Grandpa’s Respect
pitch: Turn a chess game photo into an exact board, 20-move analysis, and your best shot at finally earning Grandpa’s respect. all in browser.
about_excerpt: Turn a chess game photo into an exact board, 20-move analysis, and your best shot at finally earning Grandpa’s respect. all in browser. Like Comment Story Updates Chinese Chess WebMCP: How to Win Grandpa's Respect Inspiration You see a Chinese chess match on TV, or two people playing in the park. You wonder what is happening and which move is better. Even a powerful AI may struggle to reconstruct every piece from a screen or photograph, and the image alone cannot reveal what a real chess engine sees many moves ahead. That everyday problem gave us the idea for Chinese Chess WebMCP. Many AI integrations help agents search across more information. We wanted to explore the complementary problem: going deeper into one interactive system, then making that depth easy for anyone to use. What it does Chinese Chess WebMCP is an interactive Chinese chess board with an actual chess engine running inside the browser. Through WebMCP, an AI agent can call the page for the exact position, legal moves, ranked candidate moves, scores, principal variations, and visible board annotations. The workflow can begin with the board already on the page or with a photograph of a real game. The AI converts the image into a proposed position, the page validates it, and the user confirms the result. From there, the same position becomes available for reliable engine analysis. The answer does not have to be a blunt command to play the top move. The AI can explain why a move works, compare alternatives, coach patiently, evaluate a move the user is considering, or find the best move for a particular piece. The page provides exact state and deep computation; the AI turns them into an explanation that fits the person asking. How we built it The application is built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It includes Chinese chess rules and notation, a bilingual interface, position setup and validation, game review, and a Pikafish engine compiled to WebAssembly so analysis runs locally in the browser. The WebMCP layer registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool when the host supports it. Tool availability changes with the visible product state. For example, deep analysis is exposed only when the corresponding analysis and hint controls are enabled. Every tool execution checks that boundary again. For browsers without native WebMCP support, the page includes a visible compatibility panel that exercises the same tool contracts. GitHub Pages hosts the live demo, with a service worker providing the cross-origin isolation needed by the threaded WebAssembly engine. Challenges we ran into The photo workflow was not just an image-recognition problem. Real boards may be tilted, worn, partly obscured, or use unfamiliar handwriting. We needed a correction loop that could report invalid squares and let the AI repair only the uncertain parts instead of silently inventing a legal-looking position. The engine brought a different set of challenges. We had to reconcile board coordinates and notation, load a large neural-network file in the browser, make threaded WebAssembly work on static hosting, and present deep variations without overwhelming the user. The most important design challenge was deciding what the agent should be allowed to call. We made the WebMCP registry mirror the product's visible controls, so the agent works within the same boundary the person sees. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real Chinese chess engine runs entirely inside the browser, with no analysis backend. A photographed park or TV position can enter the same workflow as a native digital board. WebMCP exposes exact state and multi-move search, not a fragile interpretation of pixels. The AI can turn one structured result into direct advice, patient coaching, comparisons, move checking, or visible arrows on the board. The application is bilingual, open source, and available as a live demo with reproducible local tests. What we learned The most useful agent interface is not always the one with the most data. Sometimes the missing ingredient is depth: access to state and computation that exists inside an application but cannot be recovered reliably from its pixels. We also learned that exposing a powerful tool is only half the design. The page needs to communicate when that tool is available, what the user has enabled, and how the result maps back to something a person can see and understand. What's next for Chinese Chess WebMCP: How to Win Grandpa's Respect Next, we want to improve photo recognition across more board styles and camera angles, make the correction loop faster, and add richer coaching personalities without changing the underlying analysis. We also want to test the native WebMCP flow with more hosts as the API evolves, while keeping the in-page tool panel useful for anyone who wants to inspect the contracts today.
